paragraphs: Even before the war, however, the equilibrium established between old civilizations and new resources was under threat. Europe's prosperity rested on two facts. First, owing to America's large exportable surplus of foodstuffs, Europe could buy food cheaply, measured in terms of the labour needed to produce her own exports. Second, as a result of her earlier investments of capital, she was entitled to a substantial sum every year without any payment in return. The second of these factors then seemed out of danger. The first, however, was less secure, because of the growth of population overseas, chiefly in the United States.

When the virgin soils of America first came into bearing, the population of those continents, and therefore their local requirements, were very small compared with those of Europe. As lately as 1890, Europe had three times the population of North and South America together. But by 1914, the domestic requirements of the United States for wheat were approaching its production. The day was evidently near when there would be an exportable surplus only in years of exceptionally favourable harvest. Indeed, present American requirements are estimated at more than ninety per cent of the average yield of the five years 1909 to 1913. At that time, however, the tendency towards stringency showed itself not so much as a lack of abundance but as a steady rise in real cost. Taking the world as a whole, there was no shortage of wheat. Yet to call forth an adequate supply, it was necessary to offer a higher real price. The most favourable factor was the extent to which Central and Western Europe was fed from the exportable surplus of Russia and Roumania.

In short, Europe's claim on the resources of the New World was becoming precarious. The law of diminishing returns was at last reasserting itself. Year by year, it obliged Europe to offer a greater quantity of other commodities to obtain the same amount of bread. Europe, therefore, could by no means afford the disorganization of any of her principal sources of supply.

Much more might be said in an attempt to portray the economic peculiarities of the Europe of 1914. I have chosen to emphasize the three or four greatest factors of instability. The first was an excessive population dependent for its livelihood on a complicated and artificial organization. The second was the psychological instability of the labouring and capitalist classes. The third was the instability of Europe's claim on the food supplies of the New World, coupled with the completeness of her dependence on them.

The war had shaken this system so severely as to endanger the life of Europe altogether. A great part of the Continent was sick and dying. Its population far exceeded the numbers for whom a livelihood was available. Its organization was destroyed, its transport system ruptured, and its food supplies terribly impaired.
